item.title: House prices drop in six councils in three months
item.description:
House prices drop in six councils in three months

August 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The price of homes fell in six Dutch councils in the second quarter of 2026, up from just one three months earlier, a sign that the housing market is levelling off.

Figures from national statistics agency CBS and the Land Registry showed the biggest drop was in Noord-Beveland, in Zeeland, where prices were 5.1% lower than a year earlier.

Prices also fell in Ouder-Amstel (-2.8%), Hillegom (-2.5%), Valkenswaard, Veldhoven and IJsselstein. In the first quarter, only Gulpen-Wittem in Limburg had seen a fall.

Nationally, prices were still 4.2% higher than a year earlier – the tenth quarter in a row of increases, though the pace has slowed.

The sharpest rises were in the rural east and north. Prices in Oost Gelre, in Gelderland, jumped 20.9%, followed by Voorst (19.4%) and Pekela (16.2%).

Among the four biggest cities, prices in Amsterdam rose 0.1%.

item.title: Police investigating three explosive attacks on pilates studio
item.description:
Police investigating three explosive attacks on pilates studio

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A pilates studio in Gelderland has been hit by three explosive attacks in six weeks, the most recent in the early hours of Monday, police have said.

The studio in Zevenaar, which opened a year ago, was first targeted on June 24, when a blast blew a window pane out of the front door and caused a fire to break out.

A witness saw a man in black clothing and a cap running from the scene immediately after the explosion, but police have not managed to trace him.

Five days later a second explosion blew a hole in the entrance. The word betalen (“pay”) was written three times on a window.

The most recent attack was at around 2.45am on Monday, when another explosion went off and a brick was hurled through a window, Omroep Gelderland reported. The explosion was heard throughout the neighbourhood.

The door and several windows of the building have been boarded up following the attacks. Police would not say if they were linked or if any arrests have been made.

item.title: Two men suspected of helping grave robber sell stolen valuables

Two men suspected of helping grave robber sell stolen valuables

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Two men have been questioned on suspicion of acting as accomplices for a man accused of stealing valuables from a cemetery in The Hague by selling the items to a gold dealer.

The 60-year-old man, who works as a shift manager at the city’s main cemetery on Kerkhoflaan, was arrested in June after police received a tip-off that items such as jewellery and gold fillings had been stolen during working hours.

The prosecution service confirmed on Monday that two other people who worked at the cemetery were suspected of money laundering “by selling valuable objects originating from the cemetery”.

The man was arrested after an inspection of the official register where second-hand and antique traders are required to log their purchases revealed that he had sold several items to a gold exchange bureau.

Prosecutors said there were no indications from the investigation so far that items had been stolen from other cemeteries in the city. The inquiry covers the period from 2023 until the man’s arrest.

The city council has launched its own internal inquiry and set up a hotline for families who were concerned that their relatives’ valuables may have been stolen. So far the hotline has received around 60 calls.

item.title: Scammers flood TikTok with fake student rental ads
item.description:
Scammers flood TikTok with fake student rental ads

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Hundreds of fake advertisements for student rooms and rental homes are circulating on TikTok in an effort to defraud people looking for housing, according to an investigation by broadcaster NOS.

The scammers are also lifting listings from Pararius, one of the largest rental platforms in the Netherlands, and the company says it now wants TikTok to act. “We are completely fed up and want action from TikTok now,” Jasper de Groot, a Pararius spokesperson, told the broadcaster.

Some of the people who lose money come to Pararius believing they have rented through the site, De Groot said, because they have transferred a payment – only for it to reach a scammer instead.

Scams and complaints 
The fraudsters copy photographs of real rooms from Pararius and reuse them in fake posts. Victims are typically asked to pay before they can view a property – a deposit, a viewing fee or a “reservation guarantee” – after which the money disappears.

The national student union, the LSVb, said it regularly hears from young people who get conned out of their money. “Sometimes a deposit is also demanded in advance and the room turns out not to exist at all,” said vice-chair Juliana Könning. “Students then lose their deposit of, say, three months’ rent.”

The Fraudehelpdesk, the national fraud reporting centre, received 175 reports in the first half of 2026 from people scammed through an advertisement, NOS Stories said, up from 21 in the previous six months.

International students are among those most exposed, unable to fall back on a parental home and often unfamiliar with their rights, the LSVb has warned in the past.

Platforms under pressure
TikTok said content used to defraud people is not allowed and that it removes such posts. The platform did not explain why it had not acted on the reports filed by Pararius.

After NOS Stories shared a number of fake advertisements, the accounts behind them were taken down, but dozens of other scam accounts remained online.

Pararius said it had sent TikTok dossiers containing victims’ police reports and a registered letter, without success, and would take legal action against the platform. “It has to stop,” De Groot said.

Funda said it warns consumers but can do little because the fraud takes place elsewhere, while room-rental site Kamernet said it advises users to report suspicious posts and may pursue legal steps if they are not removed.

item.title: Perks of the job: making the most of your Dutch salary
item.description:
Partner content

Perks of the job: making the most of your Dutch salary

August 10, 2026

So you’ve got the job, you are moving to the Netherlands and you are ready to jump into your new life. Here is a guide from ABN Amro on some practical and financial matters you need to arrange, as well as some Dutch workplace benefits worth knowing about. 

Get your finances set up

First things first – you need a current account so your employer can deposit your salary, and having a local account will make it easier to manage your day-to-day finances. Note, you must have a Dutch bank account to get paid by a Dutch employer.

ABN Amro, which has 25 years’ experience in helping expat clients, is currently offering up to €175 cashback to new account holders – a handy financial bonus, especially at the start of a new life in the Netherlands.

But what other financial things do you need to get sorted out? Apart from a current account, you might like to start saving, so opening a savings account at the same bank would be a sensible move.

You’ll also need insurance – you’ll find out very soon that the Dutch love insurance – and, of course, some insurance, such as health cover, is compulsory too. ABN Amro offers several insurance products that you should consider – from personal liability to contents and legal aid. If you take out three or more insurance policies with them, you will receive a 3% to 5% package discount. That’s another nice financial bonus.

Then there are work-related financial benefits.

Exploring Dutch employee benefits

One perk of a Dutch job that many people are not aware of to begin with is holiday pay, or vakantiegeld. All workers and benefit claimants in the Netherlands have the right to holiday pay, which is equivalent to 8% of their annual income.

The concept of holiday pay dates back to 1910 and the money was traditionally paid out at the end of May to make sure people actually used it to pay for a break.

By the way, by law you are entitled to at least 20 paid holiday days if you work a five-day week, but in most pay deals (CAOs), 25 paid days off or even more are the norm.

In some sectors you may also be entitled to a 13th month paid out in December. Some companies also have different ways of giving their staff a bonus, such as a fixed amount for reaching a performance target.

Travel allowances and company bikes

Your job may entitle you to help with the cost of getting to and from work. Employers are allowed to give staff a tax-free allowance of 23 cents per kilometre for using public transport or a car or bike to commute, or you may be entitled to a public transport card that offers discounted travel. You may even be able to get a company bike.

Every employer is different, so make sure you ask HR about the travel perks at your company.

Other job-related perks

You may find your company canteen is subsidised or even free. You may also be entitled to gym membership or other club activities, and by law, if you work remotely, you are entitled to €2.45 a day as a working-from-home allowance. Some companies also offer a training budget to keep your skills up to date or provide Dutch lessons for their international staff.

Many internationals are surprised by the extra payments and perks they are entitled to when working for a Dutch company, just as they are surprised by the strict Dutch work-life balance and the way most people head off home at 5pm and don’t answer their work phone at the weekend.

Make sure you don’t get any unwanted financial surprises by getting your money matters sorted out, and do feel free to put your questions to ABN Amro’s specialist support staff for internationals. Find out more about opening an ABN Amro bank account and how you can benefit from a €175 cashback offer. That’s a lot of takeaway lattes – also an essential part of Dutch working life!

item.title: Rotterdam night entry ban brings quiet, residents want it kept
item.description:
Rotterdam night entry ban brings quiet, residents want it kept

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Residents of the Rotterdam neighbourhood De Esch say the nights have been quiet since a ban on entering the area took effect two weeks ago, but fear the disruption will return when it runs out in October.

A curfew for anyone without a good reason for being in the area was imposed on July 23, making it an offence to be on the streets from 11pm till 5am. The unprecedented move follows years of persistent anti-social behaviour in the area, usually by people who don’t live there.

Police stopped about 100 people during the first fortnight, though no fines have been issued yet – the penalty is expected to be more than €100.

Quiet nights
“The windows can just stay open all the time,” one resident told broadcaster NOS. “It was very quiet from night one.”

Another resident told regional broadcaster Rijnmond that before the ban she had been kept awake almost every night by shouting and car horns, even with earplugs, and had slept well for the first time in a long while.

The neighbourhood, home to more than 4,000 people, had put up with street races, drug use and prostitution at night for years. Police research found that most of those responsible came from outside De Esch.

Police and the council say the disruption has not moved to other areas, but both note that it is the holiday season and the picture may change.

After October
The ban runs for three months and can be extended by another three after consultation.

The residents’ committee wants the neighbourhood closed at night once it ends, with marshals at the entrances at weekends letting in only people with a reason to be there.

The neighbourhood council, which advises the city, is against that. “It restricts the movement of other Rotterdammers too much,” its chairman Christiaan de Jong told NOS.

He said he hoped instead that behaviour would change and the disruption would be less than before. The council says it is too early to discuss a permanent solution, and that no other part of Rotterdam needs the same measure.

item.title: German zeppelin takes to Dutch skies to measure air pollution
item.description:
German zeppelin takes to Dutch skies to measure air pollution

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

People living in the Veluwe region near the German border have been surprised by the sight of a zeppelin hovering in the skies above their heads.

The airship took off from Essen, in the Ruhr area of North Rhine-Westphalia, and is being used to measure air pollution in an area on both sides of the border that covers Arnhem and Utrecht.

Scientists from Wageningen University & Research have equipped the balloon with instruments to measure levels of CO2 pollution, emissions and fine particles in the air, in a joint operation with German colleagues.

“The substances are partly produced by the forest and partly by traffic and industry,” researcher Michiel van der Molen told NOS. “Exactly how that works and how quickly it spreads is interesting, but mostly unknown.”

The zeppelin is due to pass over the area several times during the next week at a height of around 300 metres above ground level. Its path can be followed on Flightradar24 under the code DLZFN.

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Thieves broke into a police station in The Hague to try to retrieve a batch of illegal cigarettes that were seized in a raid on Friday.

Four suspects were arrested when they were caught while trying to throw boxes of cigarettes over the fence of the police compound on Zichtenburglaan at 4.45am on Saturday.

One of the boxes caught on the fence and burst open, scattering cigarettes over the ground just as officers arrived on the scene.

The suspects tried to escape by car, but were forced off the road and arrested within 15 minutes later. One man was injured and taken to hospital under a police escort.

The haul of 1.2 million cigarettes was confiscated on Mandelastraat in Delft on Friday. Earlier in the week police recovered 500,000 iillegal cigarettes in two vans in the town.

Officers are investigating whether the break-in at the police station is linked to the earlier raids in Delft.

The A12 motorway heading out of The Hague was briefly closed on Monday morning following a crash involving six cars.

The multiple pile-up happened near the Prins Clausplein junction at Nootdorp at around 10am. Police are investigating the cause.

Two ambulances were seen at the scene, but no details have been released about whether any drivers or passengers were injured.

Traffic in the Utrecht direction was diverted via the A20 and A13 via Rotterdam. One lane has since reopened.

item.title: Military intelligence chief exposed his home address on Strava
item.description:
Military intelligence chief exposed his home address on Strava

August 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The head of the Netherlands’ military intelligence service (MIVD) kept a public account on the fitness app Strava for years, allowing anyone to follow his cycling and running routes and work out where he lived, the Volkskrant reported on Friday.

Peter Reesink, a vice-admiral who has led the MIVD since February 2024, had logged activities that were visible to the public between 2018 and 2025. From the routes, the paper’s reporters could establish his home address, where he stored his camper, and when and where he went on holiday.

A public account breaches the defence ministry’s guidelines. Reesink made his account private immediately after the news got out, and has requested that it be deleted.

He told the paper he had not realised the account was still active, saying he had removed the app some time ago but forgot to delete the profile.

Own warning
The lapse comes at an awkward time; in the MIVD’s 2025 annual report, Reesink warned that Russia was becoming more aggressive and that large organisations were naïve about security. He told the Volkskrant at the time that people at his own briefings still asked whether they really needed to leave their phones outside.

It also comes days after the AIVD, the civilian intelligence service that works alongside the MIVD, was ranked third best in Europe in a survey of intelligence professionals.

The risks of these apps have been long established in the defence industry. In 2018, an investigation by De Correspondent and Bellingcat found that the fitness app Polar exposed the names and home addresses of thousands of military and intelligence staff worldwide, including a Dutch soldier deployed to Iraq.
